subject: Clarifying egress IP behavior, NAT pooling, and firewall timeouts for private endpoints
messages:

Cc: security@acmehealth.com
Date: Wed, 10 Feb 2027 09:12:00 -0800
Subject: Private endpoint egress - need clarification and concrete IPs

Hi Michael / Laura,

Thanks again for the walkthrough yesterday. Our security team asked for a concise list of egress constraints we need to enforce on our firewall for the Redwood private control plane and data egress path. Specifically:

- Exact public IPs (or small CIDRs) clients will appear from when reaching Redwood hosted services (control plane callbacks, license checks, telemetry).
- Whether Redwood requires TCP/443 only, or additional ports (e.g., 5222, 8443 for agent telemetry).
- Clarification on whether TLS is terminated at our edge or at Redwood, and whether mutual TLS (mTLS) is required.
- Guidance on NAT pooling: will connections be source-NATed from a small predictable pool, or do you rely on ephemeral egress IPs per host?

We also need a firewall rule template (deny-by-default example with needed allow rules) and a short diagram we can attach to the audit packet. Can you send these by EOD PST? Our procurement is waiting on the SOC/secure-connect checklist to move the contract forward.

Appreciate it,
Jessica

CISO, Acme Health

From: Michael Grant <michael.grant@redwood.ai>

Subject: RE: Private endpoint egress - need clarification and concrete IPs

Jessica,

Short summary first, details below and attached files for your ops packet.

- Ports/protocols: outbound FROM your VPC/NAT -> TO Redwood: TCP/443 (HTTPS) only. No additional application ports are required for standard private deployments.
- TLS: TLS (1.2+) is terminated at Redwood. We support optional mutual TLS for customers who require certificate-based identity; enable on request.
- Egress IPs (hosted control plane): 35.183.72.128/29 (primary) and 18.204.34.64/28 (secondary). See attached egress_ip_ranges.csv.
- NAT behavior: For hosted control plane traffic we present a small, stable pool of NAT IPs (the CIDRs above). We do not depend on ephemeral per-host public addresses for callbacks or streaming. If you operate a corporate proxy/NAT gateway, give us the outbound public IP(s) and we will add them to our allowlist checks.

Attached: redwood_private_endpoint_network_diagram.pdf, egress_ip_ranges.csv, firewall-rule-template.yaml

Recommended firewall snippet (deny-by-default):
- Policy: Default deny all outbound except allowlist
- Allow: source: <your-agent-subnets> -> dest: 35.183.72.128/29, ports: TCP 443, application: TLS
- Allow: source: <your-nat-gateway-ip(s)> -> dest: 18.204.34.64/28, ports: TCP 443 (backup/control callbacks)
- DNS: allow UDP/TCP 53 from NAT gateway to your resolvers only
- Monitoring: log and alert on TLS handshake failures and excessive connection reset rates

If you require streaming low-latency sessions, we recommend permitting persistent CONNECT/keepalive flows to the primary CIDR.

Happy to sign a short addendum for your audit. Let us know if you want a 30-min netops call.

Thanks,
Michael Grant
Head of Product Ops, Redwood Inference

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>
To: security@acmehealth.com, Michael Grant <michael.grant@redwood.ai>, laura.bennett@redwood.ai
Date: Thu, 11 Feb 2027 13:45:00 -08:00
Subject: RE: Private endpoint egress - need clarification and concrete IPs

Hi all,

Technical clarifications from the runtime/network team:

- CIDR role split: 35.183.72.128/29 is the primary pool we use for long-lived streaming (LLC) and session-based connections. The 18.204.34.64/28 pool is intended primarily for short-lived control plane callbacks, license checks, and webhook-style requests. We documented that split to help customers set different conntrack rules if desired.
- Conntrack/idle timeouts: for streaming we recommend firewall conntrack idle >= 20 minutes (1200s). For short HTTP callbacks a 6020s timeout is reasonable.
- Keepalive: set TCP keepalive on NAT gateway/proxy to 90s with at least 3 probes; Redwood agents use HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 with application-level pings where applicable.
- Source IP reuse: in our hosted control plane the pools are shared across customers in the same region. IPs are NOT uniquely dedicated to a single customer by default. If your compliance requires dedicated egress IPs, we can provision a dedicated NAT IP (or small /32 set) as part of an enterprise addendum.
- Sticky behavior: streaming sessions are pinned to a NAT translation for the life of the session; you should not see mid-session source-IP changes unless your NAT device recycles connections.

Operational notes:
- If you have very strict connection-count or tracking limits, we can provide a per-hour estimate of concurrent connections for your planned fleet so you can size timeouts and conntrack table entries.
- For corporate proxies: ensure SSL/TLS CONNECT is permitted to the CIDRs and that proxy does not terminate TLS (unless you are doing device-in-the-middle inspection; in that case we need to coordinate cert chains).

Happy to share the traffic profile numbers in a separate file for capacity planning.

Regards,
Karthik Iyer
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference

Jessica / Team,

Following up: we can enable mTLS for your account and will generate a client certificate bundle if you want certificate-based mutual authentication. If you choose mTLS, steps are:
1) Redwood issues client cert + CA chain (PEM)
2) Your proxy/firewall will present the client cert on outbound connections to Redwood (or your NAT device must not strip it)
3) We validate the cert on connection and tie it to your account.

I'll attach a short provisioning guide and a sample firewall ACL you can paste into your change request. We're available for a 30-min netops call to walk through the addendum and signatures we need for the audit packet.

I'll also prepare the signed addendum confirming the CIDRs above are used for control/streaming traffic and not for unrelated third-party services.

Irene Choi
Security & Compliance, Redwood Inference
